analysis.one_liner: Requires high-risk chemical plants to assess vulnerability to attack and use safer designs to prevent toxic releases.
analysis.headline: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate calendar on Nov. 15, 2002, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced weeks after the September 11 attacks, the bill would have directed the EPA to identify the chemical facilities and substances that pose the greatest danger to nearby communities, national security, and critical infrastructure. Owners and operators of those facilities would have to assess their vulnerability to terrorist attack or other unauthorized release, identify hazards, and file prevention, preparedness, and response plans — including safer design and maintenance such as inherently safer technology, containment, security measures, and buffer zones near homes and schools. The EPA and Attorney General could seek court orders against imminent dangers, backed by civil and criminal penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near high-risk chemical facilities — including water treatment plants, refineries, and industrial chemical sites storing large quantities of toxic substances like chlorine. The bill required facilities to consult local law enforcement, first responders, and employees when assessing and planning, so emergency responders and plant workers would also have gained better information and protections.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA would designate the highest-risk combinations of facilities and substances based on severity of potential harm, proximity to population centers, threats to national security, and threats to critical infrastructure.

Owners and operators of high-priority facilities must conduct vulnerability assessments to terrorist attack, identify hazards from an unauthorized release, and prepare prevention, preparedness, and response plans, certifying them to the EPA within set deadlines.

Required plans must include safer design and maintenance — inherently safer technology that uses less hazardous substances or smaller quantities, maintained containment and mitigation equipment, security measures like intrusion detection and background checks, and buffer zones separating plants from residences, schools, hospitals, and shopping areas, each to the extent practicable.

The EPA or Attorney General could secure court relief or issue orders to abate imminent and substantial endangerments from a potential release, with civil penalties up to $25,000 per day and criminal fines and imprisonment for knowing violations.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of high-priority chemical facilities, who would bear the cost of vulnerability assessments, written plans, security upgrades, and potentially process redesign to use less hazardous substances or smaller quantities of dangerous chemicals. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers, and federal agencies would need funding to write regulations and review the submitted plans.

drawbacks.text: The reported version weakened the original bill: 'safer design and maintenance' — including inherently safer technology — must be implemented only 'to the extent practicable,' and EPA compliance certifications would merely record a checklist showing a facility considered the four safer-design elements rather than force specific changes.

The reported version exempts all vulnerability assessments and prevention plans submitted to the EPA from public disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, so communities near a facility could not see what hazards were found there.

The reported version leads with compliance assistance: before the EPA can order a facility to comply, it must first give advice and technical assistance and then wait 30 days, and owners face civil penalties only for violating orders — a slower enforcement path than the introduced version's direct abatement authority.

The bill narrowed between introduction and committee report: the original covered vessels, trucks, rail cars, and containers holding dangerous substances, while the reported version covers only stationary industrial sources, and the original's blanket public access to records with narrow exceptions became a near-total disclosure exemption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is compliance expense for facility owners against reduced risk of a catastrophic toxic release near populated areas — a risk the bill's findings called a serious threat to public health and critical infrastructure. The version that cleared committee was significantly softer than the one introduced: safer technology became a factor to 'consider' rather than a duty, plans were shielded from public view, and enforcement started with assistance rather than orders. An honest supporter would acknowledge the reported bill promised far less protection than the original, though it still established the first mandatory federal security assessments for high-risk chemical plants.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved the bill with an amendment in July 2002 and formally reported it to the Senate calendar on November 15, 2002, but the Senate never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2003, so it died without ever reaching a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Corzine introduced the bill on October 31, 2001, three weeks after the September 11 attacks, 'to help protect the public against the threat of chemical attacks.'
The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee held a hearing on the bill in its Superfund and Waste Management subcommittee on November 14, 2001.
On July 25, 2002, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On November 15, 2002, the committee, chaired by Sen. Jeffords, formally reported the bill with a substitute amendment and written report No. 107-342, with additional views filed.
The reported bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 764 — the waiting list for bills eligible for floor consideration — on November 15, 2002.

The substitute amendment replaced the introduced bill's mandatory safer-technology duty with a certification-and-review system, exempted assessments and plans from FOIA, and limited coverage to stationary sources.
No floor vote ever occurred before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill received no further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and operators of high-risk chemical facilities came out ahead: they avoided mandatory vulnerability assessments, prevention plans, per-day penalties, and any pressure toward inherently safer technology for the rest of the Congress. Communities near those plants gained nothing, and no federal chemical security mandate existed as of the Congress's end.

for.name: Sen. Jon Corzine
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 31, 2001, weeks after the September 11 attacks, and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Sen. James Jeffords
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing on the bill in November 2001, ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in July 2002, and formally reported it to the Senate calendar in November 2002.

for.name: Sens. Barbara Boxer, Hillary Clinton, and Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Joined Corzine in introducing the bill in the Senate.

against.name: Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor schedule in the session's final weeks and never brought the reported bill up for a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Chemical industry (led by the American Chemistry Council)
against.role: Trade association for U.S. chemical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against legislated chemical security mandates, arguing for voluntary industry security measures instead of requirements including inherently safer technology.

against.name: Republican members of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Minority members of the reporting committee
against.what_they_did: Filed additional views when the committee reported the bill on November 15, 2002.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent, the bill cleared committee under an independent chairman, and no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested on the floor; the only recorded dissent was 'additional views' filed by committee members.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and operators of high-risk facilities (refineries, water treatment, industrial chemical plants)
industries.note: The bill would have required vulnerability assessments, prevention plans, and safer design — potentially including inherently safer technology — at facilities the EPA designates high priority, backed by penalties up to $25,000 per day for violating orders. Its interest in the bill ran against the public's, because avoiding those requirements was the industry's gain while nearby communities went without mandated protection when the bill died.
